So far, India has done well in navigating Trump 2.0. Delhi and
Washington must find an equilibrium that benefits both
TRADE WAR, an upending of the US's traditional relationships with its
Westem European allies, a polarising immigration policy, attacks on the
A established liberal order — Donald Trump's first 100 days in office have
marked a disruption of the international systems, and presented a chal-
lenge to countries like India that must navigate the consequent uncertainties, To under-
stand the impact and to try and anticipate what the future holds, it'simportant to look at
the ideological shift in US domestic politics under Trump, and the issues that matter to
his political base. Trump's attack on the global trading system that has served the US so
well for decades is about catering to those left behind by globalisation and those suffer-
ing from a rising inequality. Second, many Trump supporters are tired of America’s “se-
curitycommitments” abroad, which they see as having led the country intocostly and pro-
tracted conflicts, Third, among some sections, there was the impression that immigration
policies had become too liberal and that a new balance needed to be struck. Fourth,
Trump’s politics has targeted “wokeism”, which it sought to present as an elite concer.
Itis across these four registers that the most controversial of Trump's moves — and some
would say, excesses — have taken place. The backlash from liberal circles is underway,
but it remains to be seen whether it can pose a credible political challenge.
Delhi has had to navigate the TrumpAdministration’s policies on trade and immigration,
and now, increasingly, global security. On each, it has managed to play aholding game and,
in many cases, made progress. India has been circumspect on Washington's tariff regime,
choosing to work behind thescenes rather than engage in biuster on theintemational stage.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi was among the first world leaders tovisit the White House
in Trump 2.0, and US Vice President J D Vance’s India trip earlier this month cemented the
gains from the Modi-Trump meeting, The Terms of Reference for a trade deal have been fi-
nalised, and it isin the interest of both countries to firm it up soonerratherthan later. Onthe
security front, Washington seems eager to support partners with whom it shares interests
and who, in turn, are willing to work with it. Given that India is not anally and is looking for
like-minded partners in the Indo-Pacific, the US’s new outlook could workinits favour. On
immigration, Delhi has accepted deportation of illegal immigrants while trying to protect
the visa regimes that allow technology workers and other skilled labour to remain in America.
The challenge in the next 100 days will be to find an equilibrium that benefits both
India and the US. There is some reason to be optimistic. Both Trump and Vance have re-
iterated the importance of the Quad and India’s role in it. The lack of equivocation vis-
a-vis Pakistan inthe aftermath of the terrorist attack in Pahalgam is also a welcome sign,
as was the deportation earlier of Tahawwur Rana, the Pakistani-Canadian doctor in-
volved in the Mumbai attacks. Moving forward, the understanding Delhi and Washington
evidently share on security cooperation must be expanded to other areas, especially bi-
lateral trade and immigration.

articles.deck_raw:
As Trump’s trade policies cause fluctuations in markets, the
near-term outlook remains uncertain
articles.body_raw:
VER THE PAST month, stock markets in India and around the world have
seen a high degree of volatility. On April 2, when US President Donald
() Trump announced his policy of reciprocal tariffs, the Dow plunged 1,450
points or 3.4 per cent. Markets around the world tanked. By April 7, the
BSE Sensex had fallen to 73,137, down from 76,617 on April 2. Over the same period, Brent
crude oil fell from $74.95 per barrel to $64.4, But, in the days and weeks after, global mar-
kets recovered, although partially, and the Sensex reclaimed the 80,000 level. On Monday,
it ended the day at 80,218, up 2.2 percent year-to-date.
The sharp upturn in global markets has been attributed to Trump pausing the impo-
sition of higher tariffs, allowing countries to negotiate deals with the US. The possibility
of early conclusion of an India-US trade deal — US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is re-
ported to have said that India could well be the first country to sign one — has buoyed sen-
timent in India. The dollar is also weakening. The dollar index — which measures the
strength of the greenback against a basket of currencies — has fallen from around 111 in
January to roughly 99 now. In April, the RBI's monetary policy committee cut the bench-
mark repo rate by 25 basis points to 6 per cent, and signalled the possibility of further
easing in order to support the economy. Foreign investors have tumed optimistic over
the past few days, pouring money into the markets.
The global economy is, however, expected to slow down this year. The IMF has pegged
growth at 2.8 per cent, down 50 basis points from its earlier estimate. The Fund has also
scaled down India's growth estimate. Some analysts are, however, more pessimistic, ex-
pecting growth to slow down even more sharply. The fourth quarter results of India Inc
already point towards subdued revenue and profit growth, with weakness being ob-
served across a range of sectors, spanning consumption, investments and exports. For
instance, HUL saw volume and sales growth at 2 per cent and 3 per cent, respectively.
Dalmia Bharat saw volumes decline by 3 per cent, and Infosys, which saw a sequential de-
cline in revenues, has pegged revenue growth at 0-3 per cent in 2025-26. The impact of
Trump's tariffs, and the uncertainty they have unleashed, will only be visible inthe weeks
and months ahead. This will have abearing on the markets.

Now, the tables have turned: As Manchester United toil,
Liverpool's fortunes are on an upswing
\ | ANCHESTER UNITED HAVE fallen off the rails since their legendary
manager Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. Michael Jordan's Chicago Bulls
werenever the samesince his (second) retirement. Chennai Super Kings
seem to be fretting over the post-Dhoni era, if ever there will be one.
Even Liverpool had to wait for 30 very long years since Kenny Dalglish’s departure as the
manager towin England's top-division league. But they didn’t have to wait for along time
to win again, On Sunday, the Merseyside club clinched its second Premier League title in
five years. And alot of it is because they planned — and timed — the transition just right.
Jurgen Klopp, who ended Liverpool's 30-year wait in 2020, left the dub last summer
because he felt drained. Before he waved goodbye, the German left a solid team for his suc-
cessor and even had a say in picking him: Ame Slot. In his farewell speech, delivered
standing in the middle of the fabled ground, Klopp urged the club faithful to throw their
weight behind Slot. On Sunday, Slot turned to the same stands and returned the favour
by getting the fans to sing Klopp’s name. A lot of great teams would have grudgingly ad-
mired these scenes. None more so than theirarch-rivals Manchester United, whose record
of 20 titles Liverpool matched.
In the 30 years when Liverpool struggled to win the title, Manchester United clinched
half of the titlesto become the team with the highest number of English top-division tro-
phies. That record was held in high esteem because, by many metrics, the English Premier
League is regarded as the most competitive domestic club football competition in the
world The tables have now tumed. AsManchester United toil, Liverpool's fortunes are on
an upswing and the Slot machine could just be getting started.
